full_judgment:
3. The appellant herein as the pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1998 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act against pre-emptee-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and others for pre-emption of the case land. 

 5. The pre-emptee-respondents contested the case by filing written objections denying all the material statements made in the application for pre-emption. Their case, in short, is that the pre-emptor has no cause of action for filing the case. The pre-emption application is not maintainable. The case is also bad for defect of parties and is barred by limitation. The case is also barred by the principles of waiver, estoppels and acquiescence. The vendor being in need of money approached the pre-emptor to purchase the case land but he declined and at the request of the vendor, he (the pre-emptor) took him (seller) to the house of the pre-emptees, who are his close neingbours. The pre-emptor negotiated the sale of the case land by fixing the consideration of the case land in presence of witnesses. Therefore, the case is barred by principles of estoppels, waiver and acquiescence. The pre-emptor lost his right to pre-emption having refused to purchase the case land. In addition to above, he negotiated the sale in question. 

 13. The trial Court considered the evidence of P.Ws. in detail and came to a finding that they had been able to substantiate the case of the pre-emptor. The trial Court also considered the evidence of O.P.Ws.1, 2 and 3 and came to the finding that they could not prove that the pre-emptor was present at the time of settlement of price of the case land and that he was also present at the time of registration and passing of consideration money. The trial Court also found that though O.P.W.2 was declared hostile by the pre-emptees, he in cross-examination by the pre-emptor stated that he did not saw the pre-emptor on the date of registration of the disputed deed in Gopalgonj Sub-Registry Office. He also did not admit that the preemptor was offered to become a witness and that he declined to be a witness on the ground that his handwriting was not good. 

 14. The appellate Court also considered the evidence of O.P.W.4 in detail who was declared hostile by the pre-emptees. The appellate Court also found that in reply to the cross-examination of the pre-emptor, O.P.W. 4 stated that the pre-emptor was not present at the Registry Office on the date of registration of the disputed deed and also found that this O.P.W. identified the seller, Guru Das by becoming a wit-ness of the said deed. Therefore, the appellate Court held that the trial Court was justified in giving much credence to the evidence of O.P.W.4. The appellate Court, on consideration of the evidence of the witnesses of the pre-emptees, came to finding that they could not prove that the pre-emptor negotiated the sale and that he also fixed the consideration money of the case land and that he was present at the Sub-registry Office at the time of execution and registration of the disputed sale deed. 

 16. We have considered the evidence adduced by the preemptor, who deposed as P. W.1. The pre-emptor in no uncertain terms stated that he did not negotiate the sale of the disputed kabala and that his evidence was corroborated by other evidence on record. The High Court Division cannot set aside the concurrent findings of fact of the Courts below unless there is glaring misreading and non-reading of material evidence on record by the Courts below. Moreover, the trial Court always has the advantage to see the demeanour of the witnesses and the credence given by the trial Court to the evidence of a witness should not be lightly discarded by the appellate Court as well as by the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction.
